###### Abstract

The hallmark of Deep Research agents lies in compositional reasoning,
the capacity to aggregate distributed, heterogeneous information into
coherent logical insights. However, current agentic systems are often
retrieval-heavy but reasoning-light, where success is predominantly
determined by simple entity-seeking rather than the multi-step
aggregation of scattered evidence. To address this, we propose a data
synthesis pipeline WebAggregator, designed to shift the agentic paradigm
from retrieval-centric to compositional aggregation. Our approach first
employs Proactive Explorer to collect interconnected knowledge, then
Compositional Logic Proposer to weave knowledge into complex questions
using over 12 composition guidelines derived from a rigorous
deconstruction of the Deep Research problem setting. By leveraging 10K
verifiable QA pairs grounded on 50K websites, we curate a high-quality
SFT dataset via rejection sampling. Fine-tuning on this corpus
fundamentally transforms agent behavior, fostering deliberate
composition reasoning and reduced tool redundancy. The resulting
WebAggregator-32B surpasses GPT-4.1 and matches Claude-3.7-Sonnet on
GAIA, WebWalkerQA, and XBench. To address the lack of benchmarks that
emphasize both reasoning and retrieval, we introduce the WebAggregatorQA
testbed, which reveals that even with perfect retrieval, top-tier models
still underperformed. These results demonstrate that compositional
reasoning, not retrieval, is the true performance ceiling for
next-generation research agents.

## 1 Introduction

Deep Research agent systems ([OpenAI, 2025](#bib.bib11); [Monica.Im,
2025](#bib.bib25)) aim to automate scientific discovery using
foundational large language models (LLMs). Achieving this requires not
merely effective information seeking, grounding responses with accurate
knowledge, but more critically, compositional reasoning: the ability to
integrate distributed materials into coherent insights by decoding
underlying logical structures ([Bereiter and Scardamalia,
1987](#bib.bib29); [Flower and Hayes, 1981](#bib.bib19); [Mialon et al.,
2023](#bib.bib2)).

imbalance in task difficulty, which relies on search effort rather than
reasoning depth, as shown in Figure

Specifically, $`30.79\%`$ of WebWalkerQA ([Deng et al.,
2023](#bib.bib20)) and $`43.2\%`$ of TaskCraft ([Shi et al.,
2025](#bib.bib6)) tasks only require simple entity localization. This
observation aligns with other resources ([Wu et al., 2025a](#bib.bib5);
[Tao et al., 2025](#bib.bib10)), suggesting that existing tasks may not
fully test high-level reasoning. This tendency encourages agents to rely
on frequent tool execution rather than necessary reasoning steps
(Section
[4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Challenges from Compositional Reasoning ‣ 4 Analysis ‣ WebAggregator: Enhancing Compositional Reasoning Capabilities of Deep Research Agent Foundation Models")),
leaving compositional reasoning as a critical but underexplored
frontier.

To bridge these gaps, we introduce WebAggregator, an automated framework
designed to generate verifiable training data that pushes agents beyond
information seeking towards deep compositional reasoning (Figure
[3](#S1.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ WebAggregator: Enhancing Compositional Reasoning Capabilities of Deep Research Agent Foundation Models"))
. The workflow consists of two phases: the Proactive Explorer and the
Compositional Logic Proposer. Equipped with a comprehensive toolkit,
spanning search, static parsing, dynamic interaction, file processing,
and visual perception, the agent is capable of navigating in realistic
web environments. Proactive Explorer initiates exploration from anchor
URLs to autonomously gather interconnected resources. Subsequently, the
Compositional Logic Proposer synthesizes complex tasks that explicitly
necessitate multi-hop aggregation operations across these collected
materials. Drawing on prior multi-hop reasoning studies ([Chang et al.,
2022](#bib.bib30); [Yang et al., 2018](#bib.bib17); [Talmor et al.,
2021](#bib.bib7); [Wu et al., 2025c](#bib.bib23); [Wong et al.,
2025](#bib.bib33)), this module employs a rigorous taxonomy categorized
into Element, Set, Scientific Analysis, and Temporal Reasoning, which
are further refined into 12 granular subtypes (Table
[4](#A0.T4 "Table 4 ‣ WebAggregator: Enhancing Compositional Reasoning Capabilities of Deep Research Agent Foundation Models"))
to tailor the system to the analytical depth required by Deep Research.

![Refer to caption](2510.14438v2/illus.png)

Figure 3: Pipeline of WebAggregator for WebAggregatorQA construction.
(1) Proactive Explorer gathers comprehensive information by interacting
with the web environment through tools (more details in Figure
[10](#A2.F10 "Figure 10 ‣ QA Alignment-based Filtering ‣ B.1 More Explanations of Quality Control ‣ Appendix B More Details for WebAggregatorQA ‣ WebAggregator: Enhancing Compositional Reasoning Capabilities of Deep Research Agent Foundation Models")).
(2) Compositional Logic Proposer synthesizes QA pairs based on the
collected knowledge by instantiating the high-level composition guidance
into concrete operations, e.g., Statistic Analysis $`\rightarrow`$
standard deviation.

We utilize WebAggregator to construct WebAggregatorQA, a dataset of
approximately 10K QA pairs designed to enforce rigorous compositional
reasoning. As illustrated in Figure
[2](#S1.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ WebAggregator: Enhancing Compositional Reasoning Capabilities of Deep Research Agent Foundation Models"),
WebAggregatorQA are designed to be non-trivial. Even with all necessary
references provided, an agent must perform genuine compositional
reasoning to derive the answer, rather than relying on direct
extraction. Our rigorous quality control ensures the resulting tasks
demand genuine compositional reasoning rather than shallow pattern
matching. By leveraging rejection sampling to train the WebAggregator
model family, we demonstrate the high effectiveness of this training
corpus. Extensive experiments on GAIA, WebWalkerQA, and XBench show that
WebAggregator-8B significantly surpasses GPT-4.1, while the 32B variant
outperforms all strong baselines. Furthermore, fine-tuning on
WebAggregatorQA fundamentally improves agent behavior by encouraging
deeper reasoning steps and clearly reducing redundant tool usage,
leading to robust performance gains.

The manually annotated WebAggregatorQA test set serves as a challenging
benchmark, where even Claude-3.7-Sonnet achieves only 28.3%. Crucially,
our error analysis reveals a critical limitation: accurate reference
retrieval does not guarantee task success. Even with the full reference
context provided, Claude-3.7-Sonnet scores only 42.1%, highlighting
severe challenges in compositional reasoning. Our further analysis
attributes this failure to gaps in advanced agentic capabilities, such
as ineffective self-refinement, and faulty information utilization.
These findings underscore the enduring value of WebAggregatorQA as a
testbed, suggesting that future progress must transcend
retrieval-centric paradigms to foster agents capable of the rigorous
compositional reasoning required for complex tasks.

## 2 WebAggregator

We aim to automatically synthesize scalable, challenging QA pairs
grounded in real web resources, requiring minimal human involvement.
Unlike fact-lookup puzzles [Wei et al. (2025)](#bib.bib15); [Wu et al.
(2025b)](#bib.bib3), these tasks demand both complex retrieval and
compositional reasoning. We propose an automatically verifiable
pipeline, WebAggregator (Figure
[3](#S1.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ WebAggregator: Enhancing Compositional Reasoning Capabilities of Deep Research Agent Foundation Models")),
that frames synthesis as an agentic task:¹¹ 1 Agent details in Appendix
[A](#A1 "Appendix A Agent Structure ‣ WebAggregator: Enhancing Compositional Reasoning Capabilities of Deep Research Agent Foundation Models").
starting from anchor URLs, Proactive Explorer harvests interconnected
information from diversified sources, which is formulated by
Compositional Logic Proposer into reasoning-intensive QAs, which then
undergo rigorous automated quality control.

### 2.1 Anchor URL Collection

By selecting seed URLs across multiple domains, we can effectively
regulate the dataset’s domain distribution, thereby enabling effective
distribution balance. We sampled 5,000 topic-diverse queries from QA and
scientific datasets ([Yang et al., 2018](#bib.bib17); [Jin et al.,
2019](#bib.bib21); [Trivedi et al., 2022](#bib.bib22)) and retrieved
URLs via Google Search, resulting in over 160,000 anchor links from 11+
domains (Figure
[4](#S2.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 2.2.1 Proactive Explorer ‣ 2.2 WebAggregator: From Exploration to Composition ‣ 2 WebAggregator ‣ WebAggregator: Enhancing Compositional Reasoning Capabilities of Deep Research Agent Foundation Models")).

### 2.2 WebAggregator: From Exploration to Composition

In this section, we introduce our approach to synthesizing target QA
pairs by framing task synthesis as a specialized form of web-agent
tasks. The agent is given a task prompt consisting of two components:
Proactive Explorer and Compositional Logic Proposal, enabling it to
complete the task construction in an end-to-end manner.

#### 2.2.1 Proactive Explorer

Proactive Explorer aims to collect diverse information as the foundation
for task construction by exploration on the real web. During this phase
(Figure
[3](#S1.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ WebAggregator: Enhancing Compositional Reasoning Capabilities of Deep Research Agent Foundation Models")),
the agent is prompted to start from a single anchor URL and employ
various tools to navigate across web pages to discover any unknown but
relevant information. Interactions include navigating heterogeneous
content types such as text, files, and images, as well as dynamic
element interactions, which are still challenging for even
state-of-the-art vision language models ([Zhang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib39)). To control task difficulty and ensure the
comprehensiveness of the knowledge scope, a minimum number of web page
visits is enforced (Appendix
[B.3](#A2.SS3 "B.3 Data Construction Prompt ‣ Appendix B More Details for WebAggregatorQA ‣ WebAggregator: Enhancing Compositional Reasoning Capabilities of Deep Research Agent Foundation Models")).

![Refer to caption](2510.14438v2/domain-step.png)

Figure 4: The distribution of domains in WebAggregatorQA, tasks
categorized by the number of different tools involved during
construction, and steps (an action-observation round) in data synthesis.

This unconstrained exploration proves highly effective at sourcing
diverse information. Analysis of 5,296 exploration trajectories (Figure
[4](#S2.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 2.2.1 Proactive Explorer ‣ 2.2 WebAggregator: From Exploration to Composition ‣ 2 WebAggregator ‣ WebAggregator: Enhancing Compositional Reasoning Capabilities of Deep Research Agent Foundation Models"))
reveals significant interaction diversity. Every trajectory leverages at
least three foundational tools: Search, Visit, and ScreenShot.
Crucially, a majority of trajectories employ a wider toolkit: 48.36% use
4 distinct tools, and 28.55% use 5, while 13.41% engage with 6 or more.
This breadth of interaction enriches the knowledge pool and directly
translates into more complex downstream tasks. For instance, questions
derived from file-based information inherently test an agent’s
file-processing capabilities.

#### 2.2.2 Compositional Logic Proposer

Compositional Logic Proposer transforms raw, unstructured information
into sophisticated reasoning challenges. To systematically generate
diverse and challenging reasoning chains, we developed a taxonomy of
logical operations inspired by prior work on multi-hop and compositional
QA ([Sen et al., 2022](#bib.bib16); [Talmor et al., 2021](#bib.bib7);
[Wu et al., 2025c](#bib.bib23); [Fang et al., 2024](#bib.bib31);
[Krishna et al., 2025](#bib.bib34)). As shown in Figure
[3](#S1.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ WebAggregator: Enhancing Compositional Reasoning Capabilities of Deep Research Agent Foundation Models"),
this taxonomy is organized into four high-level categories: Element,
Set, Scientific Analysis, and Temporal Reasoning, which are further
refined into 12 granular subtypes. Element and Set operations are the
basis of compositional reasoning behaviors among knowledge snippets,
such as mathematical calculation among elements and Filtering among
sets. While Scientific Analysis and Temporal Reasoning are advanced
applications of them, involving computation-intensive and data science
tasks, to reflect real but challenging user cases.

Crucially, these 12 subtypes act as high-level conceptual guides within
the prompt, not as rigid templates. They instruct the Proposer to
instantiate these patterns into concrete, context-specific questions.
For example, Element-\>mathematical calculation guide can be
instantiated as addition, subtraction, or ratio calculation, depending
on the available data. This flexible, guided approach ensures the
generation of novel and diverse reasoning challenges (examples provided
in Table
[4](#A0.T4 "Table 4 ‣ WebAggregator: Enhancing Compositional Reasoning Capabilities of Deep Research Agent Foundation Models")).

#### 2.2.3 Quality Control

QA Alignment Checking We implement a two-stage verification process to
ensure data integrity. First, the Proposer employs a self-refinement
tool with a checklist to revise questions (Appendix
[B.5](#A2.SS5 "B.5 Prompt of Intergrated Data Quality Checking Tool ‣ Appendix B More Details for WebAggregatorQA ‣ WebAggregator: Enhancing Compositional Reasoning Capabilities of Deep Research Agent Foundation Models")).
Second, another agent reviews the data by solving it, verifying
reference URLs to guarantee strict alignment between questions, answers,
and sources (Appendix
[B.4](#A2.SS4 "B.4 Prompt of Data Quality Checking Agent ‣ Appendix B More Details for WebAggregatorQA ‣ WebAggregator: Enhancing Compositional Reasoning Capabilities of Deep Research Agent Foundation Models")).
This rigorous post-hoc filtering removes 11.72% of the initial samples.

Diversity Constraint We actively balance the dataset across domains and
compositional types.²² 2 See Appendix
[C](#A3 "Appendix C Data Contamination Analysis ‣ WebAggregator: Enhancing Compositional Reasoning Capabilities of Deep Research Agent Foundation Models")
for contamination analysis. First, we normalize the distribution of
anchor URL domains annotated by GPT-4.1 (Figure
[4](#S2.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 2.2.1 Proactive Explorer ‣ 2.2 WebAggregator: From Exploration to Composition ‣ 2 WebAggregator ‣ WebAggregator: Enhancing Compositional Reasoning Capabilities of Deep Research Agent Foundation Models")).
Second, we dynamically adjust prompts to upweight underrepresented
composition operations (e.g., calculating average) identified via
preliminary analysis. As shown in Figure
[8](#A0.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ WebAggregator: Enhancing Compositional Reasoning Capabilities of Deep Research Agent Foundation Models"),
this strategy successfully spawns diverse low-level operations tailored
to high-level guidance, such as intersection for Set tasks and table
processing for Scientific Analysis.

#### 2.2.4 Trajectory Sampling

After the task synthesis, we collect the trajectory that completes these
tasks. We utilize the agent based on GPT-4.1 with SmolAgents and collect
the plain text trajectories. To ensure the quality of the collected
trajectories, we conduct a further rejection sampling and finally
collected 6,184 trajectories for the foundation model training. (1)
Correctness: We retain those trajectories with correct predictions
according to the reference answers. (2) Format: Data with format errors
(e.g., undefined tool name or parameters) is filtered out. (3) Exception
Handling: Anomalies in observations (e.g., page failures) are kept to
improve the model’s generalization, since similar situations would occur
in the real web.

#### 2.2.5 Statistics of WebAggregatorQA

WebAggregatorQA comprises 9,883 tasks (with 200 reserved for testing),
covering 54,064 unique URLs across 12 domains. Figure
[4](#S2.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 2.2.1 Proactive Explorer ‣ 2.2 WebAggregator: From Exploration to Composition ‣ 2 WebAggregator ‣ WebAggregator: Enhancing Compositional Reasoning Capabilities of Deep Research Agent Foundation Models")
shows the distribution of domains and steps for QA construction
trajectories. Most QA pairs are constructed with around 15 steps,
demonstrating that the generated data points are not hastily created
from only a few reasoning steps, thus avoiding overly simplistic
questions.

### 2.3 WebAggregatorQA testset for Compositional Reasoning Evaluation

Existing benchmarks ([Wu et al., 2025b](#bib.bib3); [Wei et al.,
2025](#bib.bib15)) primarily assess information-seeking, often
neglecting compositional reasoning. To address this critical gap, we
introduce the test set of WebAggregatorQA, which is meticulously
annotated to evaluate both retrieval and reasoning capabilities.

Annotation Details  We uniformly split 200 tasks as seeds from
WebAggregatorQA across different domains to ensure high task diversity.
We aim to ensure every question is unambiguous, with the reference
answer correct, other candidates are verifiably incorrect. First, human
annotators solve the QA pairs, then review the QA and references to
eliminate ambiguities by adding clear constraints. To further enhance
sample reliability and reduce bias from the solver’s perspective, this
process is repeated twice: tasks are solved, ambiguities identified, and
revisions made by annotators. In the final cross-validation stage, each
question was answered by at least two annotators, yielding 155
consistently aligned samples. The other 4 samples were abandoned by
annotators due to difficulty, but their references and questions were
verified to ensure data quality and thus were retained. More details are
shown in Appendix
[B.2](#A2.SS2 "B.2 Testset Annotation ‣ Appendix B More Details for WebAggregatorQA ‣ WebAggregator: Enhancing Compositional Reasoning Capabilities of Deep Research Agent Foundation Models").

This yielded 159 samples, including those in text and multimodal,
categorized by difficulty into Level 1 (24), Level 2 (99), and Level 3
(36). Each sample contains a question, reference answer, solution, and
supporting URLs. A text example is shown in Figure
[2](#S1.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ WebAggregator: Enhancing Compositional Reasoning Capabilities of Deep Research Agent Foundation Models")
and a multimodal one is in Figure
[11](#A2.F11 "Figure 11 ‣ B.2.1 Data Collection and Verification ‣ B.2 Testset Annotation ‣ Appendix B More Details for WebAggregatorQA ‣ WebAggregator: Enhancing Compositional Reasoning Capabilities of Deep Research Agent Foundation Models").

## 3 Experiments

### 3.1 Experimental Setups

Models and Benchmarks  We construct the WebAggregator models by SFT
varied Qwen2.5 ([Yang et al., 2024](#bib.bib26)) and Qwen3 ([Yang et
al., 2025](#bib.bib24)) models on the training set of WebAggregatorQA.
We evaluate the baselines and our methods on the GAIA-text ([Mialon et
al., 2023](#bib.bib2)) following [Li et al. (2025a)](#bib.bib4); [Li et
al. (2025b)](#bib.bib9), XBench [Chen et al. (2025)](#bib.bib14),
WebWalkerQA [Wu et al. (2025b)](#bib.bib3), and WebAggregatorQA.

Training Configs  We formalize the trajectory we sampled as
$`(\text{question},a_{1},o_{1},...,a_{n},o_{n},\text{answer})`$.
$`a_{i}`$ stands for the action code the agent generated to perform tool
calling, and $`o_{i}`$ is the observation returned by the web
environment. The question and observations are masked during training.

Baselines and Metrics We mainly compare WebAggregator with three types
of prior works. a. Non-agentic foundation models that answer questions
using their internal knowledge. b. Zero-shot foundation models
initialized as agents via the SmolAgents framework. c. Strong fine-tuned
foundation models: WebThinker ([Li et al., 2025b](#bib.bib9)), WebDancer
([Wu et al., 2025a](#bib.bib5)), CognitiveKernel-Pro ([Fang et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib27)), WebSailor ([Li et al., 2025a](#bib.bib4)) and
WebShaper ([Tao et al., 2025](#bib.bib10)). We report the pass@1 and
pass@3 scores evaluated by GPT-4.1 following previous works ([Wu et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib5)).

### 3.2 Main Results

Effects of WebAggregatorQA Training Set  The experiment results are
shown in Table
[1](#S2.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 2.2.4 Trajectory Sampling ‣ 2.2 WebAggregator: From Exploration to Composition ‣ 2 WebAggregator ‣ WebAggregator: Enhancing Compositional Reasoning Capabilities of Deep Research Agent Foundation Models")
and Table
[2](#S3.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 3.1 Experimental Setups ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ WebAggregator: Enhancing Compositional Reasoning Capabilities of Deep Research Agent Foundation Models").
In the zero-shot setting, the closed-sourced models surpass Qwen models
on benchmarks. However, after tuning on WebAggregatorQA, Qwen models
exhibit clear and steady improvements on all of the benchmarks and
approach the performance of these strong baselines. Specifically, the
WebAggregator based on Qwen2.5-32B and Qwen3-32B surpasses most of the
strong baselines, including GPT-4.1 and WebShaper. The pass@3
performance of WebAggregator-32B achieves 69.9% on GAIA-text. These
observations prove the quality of WebAggregatorQA and the effectiveness
of our data construction paradigm.

Difficulty of WebAggregatorQA Test Set  The complex aggregation needs in
WebAggregatorQA pose a new challenge for current agent systems.
GPT-4.1-powered SmolAgents attain 43.7% accuracy on GAIA-text but drop
to 25.8% on WebAggregatorQA. Claude-3.7-sonnet shows a similar decline.
Furthermore, the performance gap between Claude and GPT-4.1 is smaller
on WebAggregatorQA than on GAIA-text. This suggests that for the harder
questions in WebAggregatorQA, neither model can solve them effectively,
which leads to the reduced gap. These results and our following analysis
(Section
[4](#S4 "4 Analysis ‣ WebAggregator: Enhancing Compositional Reasoning Capabilities of Deep Research Agent Foundation Models"))
highlight the substantial gap between current agent capabilities and the
demands of compositional reasoning needed for multi-hop web tasks.

Data Efficiency and Small Foundations  The construction of
WebAggregatorQA also enables highly efficient model training. By
fine-tuning Qwen3-8B on small subsets of 500 and 1,200 trajectories, we
achieve 36.9% and 38.83% accuracy on GAIA-text, respectively,
demonstrating that even limited high-quality data from WebAggregatorQA
can yield significant performance gains. This efficiency translates to
superior performance in smaller foundation models; for instance,
WebAggregator-8B achieves parity with GPT-4.1 on GAIA-text and
significantly outperforms previous baselines on WebWalkerQA and XBench
(Table
[2](#S3.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 3.1 Experimental Setups ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ WebAggregator: Enhancing Compositional Reasoning Capabilities of Deep Research Agent Foundation Models")).
Despite these gains, a performance gap persists between 8B and 32B
models on the more complex WebAggregatorQA tasks, suggesting that while
small foundations are increasingly viable and cost-effective, breaking
through the performance bottleneck of small foundations on hard tasks
remains a vital direction.

## 4 Analysis

### 4.1 Requirements for Solving WebAggregatorQA

To better understand the challenges in WebAggregatorQA, Figure
[5](#S3.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 3.1 Experimental Setups ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ WebAggregator: Enhancing Compositional Reasoning Capabilities of Deep Research Agent Foundation Models")
illustrates the distribution of information sources and the
compositional operations required for task completion.

Diversified Information Source Reliance Our analysis reveals that tasks
in WebAggregatorQA necessitate access to at least Search and Web Text.
Furthermore, these tasks frequently require information from Files,
indicating a multi-source dependency rather than reliance on a single
medium. Successfully addressing WebAggregatorQA demands advanced
web-browsing capabilities to retrieve knowledge. The benchmark proves
exceptionally challenging for models constrained by internal knowledge
alone. Even strong base models like Claude-3.7 and GPT-4.1 solve fewer
than 7% of the questions.

Diversified Composition Requirements  We observe that the compositional
reasoning requirements of WebAggregatorQA challenge the agent systems.
Figure
[5](#S3.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 3.1 Experimental Setups ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ WebAggregator: Enhancing Compositional Reasoning Capabilities of Deep Research Agent Foundation Models")
illustrates that the solving of these tasks requires diversified
composition operations, and many of them contain multiple operations. We
conduct further detailed analysis in Section
[4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Challenges from Compositional Reasoning ‣ 4 Analysis ‣ WebAggregator: Enhancing Compositional Reasoning Capabilities of Deep Research Agent Foundation Models").

### 4.2 Challenges from Compositional Reasoning

In this section, we scrutinize the behaviors of research agents and
highlight a compound challenge: compositional reasoning on the retrieved
information to derive the final answer.

Success in Seeking, Fail in Reasoning  We further investigate the impact
of compositional reasoning by analyzing a specific failure mode: perfect
reference retrieval but fails the task. In Table
[3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 4.2 Challenges from Compositional Reasoning ‣ 4 Analysis ‣ WebAggregator: Enhancing Compositional Reasoning Capabilities of Deep Research Agent Foundation Models"),
although accuracy improves when all reference URLs are visited, the
performance gain remains modest. This suggests that while successful
information retrieval is a prerequisite, the subsequent reasoning burden
remains a significant bottleneck. Notably, Qwen3-32B shows a sharp gap
between its strong retrieval and weak accuracy, highlighting a deficit
in compositional reasoning. WebAggregator-32B, however, significantly
closes this gap, reaching performance levels comparable to top-tier
baselines. Still, the lack of a high score across all models, even with
full information, underscores that the primary ceiling remains the
complex composition logic.

![Refer to caption](2510.14438v2/figs/tool-use.png)

Figure 6: Steps and tool use density of two models across test sets.
More results are shown in Table
[5](#A0.T5 "Table 5 ‣ WebAggregator: Enhancing Compositional Reasoning Capabilities of Deep Research Agent Foundation Models").

Reasoning-Intensive Nature of Composition  We evaluate the impact of
compositional reasoning on agents by analyzing their tool usage patterns
across WebAggregatorQA and WebWalkerQA in Figure
[6](#S4.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ 4.2 Challenges from Compositional Reasoning ‣ 4 Analysis ‣ WebAggregator: Enhancing Compositional Reasoning Capabilities of Deep Research Agent Foundation Models").
We define tool call density as the number of tool calls per step. We
observe that while tasks in WebAggregatorQA require more total steps to
complete, the tool call density is notably lower. This pattern suggests
that in WebAggregatorQA, models rely more heavily on reasoning steps to
execute compositional reasoning, enabling deeper synthesis and analysis
of existing information, rather than predominantly invoking tools to
acquire new external knowledge.

### 4.3 Behavior Evolution of WebAggregator

Evolution of Tool Usage Behaviors  To understand how fine-tuning on
WebAggregatorQA alters agent behavior, we analyzed their action
sequences and performed a semantic analysis on $`500`$ randomly sampled
steps per model. Following the classification by GPT-5, we categorize
internal Thought processes into: (1) Procedural & Planning (Type A):
routine instructions (e.g., "I will search for X") and state updates;
(2) Compositional Reasoning (Type B): deep operations including
information synthesis, logical deduction, and error correction. Our
findings, illustrated in Table
[5](#A0.T5 "Table 5 ‣ WebAggregator: Enhancing Compositional Reasoning Capabilities of Deep Research Agent Foundation Models")
and Figure
[9](#A0.F9 "Figure 9 ‣ WebAggregator: Enhancing Compositional Reasoning Capabilities of Deep Research Agent Foundation Models"),
reveal three key trends:

First, WebAggregators exhibit reduced tool dependency alongside enhanced
reasoning density. As shown in Table
[5](#A0.T5 "Table 5 ‣ WebAggregator: Enhancing Compositional Reasoning Capabilities of Deep Research Agent Foundation Models"),
the Reasoning Ratio (Type B) increased across all scales (e.g., from
18.6% to 26.2% for the 8B model), while Tool Call Density markedly
declined. This inverse correlation refutes the verbosity hypothesis;
rather than generating procedural fluff, the model prioritizes internal
logical synthesis over mechanical tool invocation.

Second, model scaling further amplifies evidence aggregation capacity.
Post-tuning, despite fewer tool calls, total token consumption rose by
12–17%, a growth driven exclusively by Type B reasoning. This indicates
that larger models (32B) leverage deeper internal synthesis, integrating
fragmented data into coherent insights, to resolve complex queries with
higher efficiency and fewer environment interactions.

Finally, agent behavior shifts toward a more diverse and balanced
operational distribution. Prior to tuning, tool-calling patterns were
concentrated and simplistic (e.g., 40% of trajectories relied on only
two tools, as seen in Figure
[9](#A0.F9 "Figure 9 ‣ WebAggregator: Enhancing Compositional Reasoning Capabilities of Deep Research Agent Foundation Models")).
WebAggregatorQA facilitates a transition from a retrieval-centric
paradigm to a reasoning-heavy one, prioritizing multi-step aggregation
of scattered evidence.

Evolution on Composition Reasoning Capabilities  We investigate how
model performance changes across different compositional logic types.
Logic labels are labeled by an LLM via analyzing the reference
solutions, consistent with the dataset construction method (Figure
[3](#S1.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ WebAggregator: Enhancing Compositional Reasoning Capabilities of Deep Research Agent Foundation Models")).
We compare Qwen series models before and after fine-tuning. We compute
the Phi Coefficient ($`\psi`$), measuring correlation between logic type
presence and answer correctness. More negative $`\psi`$ indicates
greater task difficulty. Figure
[7](#S4.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ 4.3 Behavior Evolution of WebAggregator ‣ 4 Analysis ‣ WebAggregator: Enhancing Compositional Reasoning Capabilities of Deep Research Agent Foundation Models")
reveals that computation-intensive logic, particularly Scientific
Analysis and Set Operations, remains the key challenge.

Figure 7: Phi Coefficients ($`\psi`$) by composition types across models
before and after tuning on WebAggregatorQA.

### 4.4 Screening of Failure Modes

To elucidate the inherent challenges of WebAggregatorQA, we conduct a
qualitative analysis of failure trajectories. We manually examine 50
representative cases from the models listed in Table
[3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 4.2 Challenges from Compositional Reasoning ‣ 4 Analysis ‣ WebAggregator: Enhancing Compositional Reasoning Capabilities of Deep Research Agent Foundation Models")
where all references were retrieved, comprising: 28 instances from
WebAggregator-32B, 6 each from Claude and GPT-4.1, and 10 additional
failure cases. We reveal a taxonomy of three failure categories:

Information Seeking Failures These errors preclude access to valid
evidence. A primary issue is Source Location Failure, where agents
misled by initial uncertainty or sub-optimal search queries, fail to
locate gold references and settle for incomplete secondary sources.

Agent Foundation Capability Failures Operational errors also derail
tasks. Common issues include Invalid Tool Calls (e.g., malformed
queries) and Exceeding Max Context, often resulting from inefficient
planning or error-correction loops.

Compositional Reasoning Failures This category covers errors during the
composition of retrieved information. (1) Faulty Composition: agents
misinterpret evidence or apply flawed reasoning, such as making
unsupported assumptions, despite accessing the correct sources (Figure
[D.1](#A4.SS1 "D.1 Example 1 ‣ Appendix D Close Screening Agent Trajectories ‣ WebAggregator: Enhancing Compositional Reasoning Capabilities of Deep Research Agent Foundation Models")).
(2) Error Accumulation: minor inaccuracies (e.g., premature rounding)
compound across steps to yield a significantly incorrect result (Figure
[D.3](#A4.SS3 "D.3 Example 3 ‣ Appendix D Close Screening Agent Trajectories ‣ WebAggregator: Enhancing Compositional Reasoning Capabilities of Deep Research Agent Foundation Models")).
(3) Ineffective Refinement: a critical failure where agents fail to
self-correct, proceeding down the erroneous logical path while being
unable to revise previous mistakes (Figure
[D.2](#A4.SS2 "D.2 Example 2 ‣ Appendix D Close Screening Agent Trajectories ‣ WebAggregator: Enhancing Compositional Reasoning Capabilities of Deep Research Agent Foundation Models")).

The above failures are rarely isolated. As shown in Figure
[D.2](#A4.SS2 "D.2 Example 2 ‣ Appendix D Close Screening Agent Trajectories ‣ WebAggregator: Enhancing Compositional Reasoning Capabilities of Deep Research Agent Foundation Models"),
an initial Faulty Composition can propagate errors downstream,
exacerbated by Ineffective Refinement. This cascade consumes the context
window (Exceeding Max Steps), increasing the probability of
hallucinations or timeouts.

## 5 Related Work

Resources for Deep Research Agents  Robust information retrieval and
precise question answering form the bedrock of deep research agents.
Consequently, developing multi-hop datasets for training agent
foundation models ([Tongyi, 2025](#bib.bib35); [Qiao et al.,
2025](#bib.bib36)) necessitates sophisticated tool-use and reasoning,
making manual construction challenging. Existing datasets like HotpotQA
([Yang et al., 2018](#bib.bib17); [Trivedi et al., 2022](#bib.bib22))
lack the complexity of authentic web interactions. While some works
synthesize request-action pairs ([Xu et al., 2025](#bib.bib28); [Chen et
al., 2024](#bib.bib8); [He et al., 2024](#bib.bib1)), they often lack
goal-oriented depth. Recent methods construct tasks from logical flows
over knowledge snippets ([Wu et al., 2025a](#bib.bib5); [Li et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib4); [Shi et al., 2025](#bib.bib6); [Xia et al.,
2025](#bib.bib32)), such as using KGs from offline pages ([Shi et al.,
2025](#bib.bib6); [Wu et al., 2025a](#bib.bib5)) or entity expansion
([Xia et al., 2025](#bib.bib32); [Tao et al., 2025](#bib.bib10)).
However, these remain limited by static content and often neglect
knowledge composition (Figure
[3](#S1.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ WebAggregator: Enhancing Compositional Reasoning Capabilities of Deep Research Agent Foundation Models")),
where complexity stems more from reasoning than entity tracing.

Benchmarking Deep Research Agents  Most existing benchmarks prioritize
information-seeking and reference filtering ([Wu et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib3); [Wei et al., 2025](#bib.bib15)), while few ([Li et
al., 2025c](#bib.bib37)) assess compositional reasoning. [Krishna et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib34) evaluates aggregation but is confined to Wikipedia,
and [Wong et al. (2025)](#bib.bib33) focuses on long sequences of simple
actions. GAIA ([Mialon et al., 2023](#bib.bib2)), though most relevant,
is becoming saturated by recent agents ([Fang et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib27); [Qiu et al., 2025](#bib.bib18)). This underscores
the need for challenging benchmarks that jointly evaluate
information-seeking and complex reasoning.

##### Training and Optimization for Research Agents

Recent advancements focus on sophisticated training and test-time
optimization. Besides standard rejection-sampling based SFT, which is
adopted in most agent post-training works ([Tongyi, 2025](#bib.bib35);
[Fang et al., 2025b](#bib.bib27); [Team et al., 2025](#bib.bib40)),
there are more advanced techniques leveraging reinforcement learning and
test-time self-evolving. In addition to simply applying the training QA
pairs as RL input queries, self-synthesized queries can be useful for
providing process-level supervision signals for better credit assignment
([Fang et al., 2025b](#bib.bib27); [Feng et al., 2025](#bib.bib41);
[Wang et al., 2026](#bib.bib42); [Li et al., 2026](#bib.bib43); [Fang et
al., 2026](#bib.bib46); [Fu et al., 2026](#bib.bib47)). More
specifically, execution errors during tool interaction can also be
converted into corrective supervision signals within the RL loop to
improve multi-turn tool robustness ([Zhang et al., 2026](#bib.bib38)).
Regarding test-time self-evolving [Fang et al. (2025a)](#bib.bib44),
synthesized data could help building agent failure taxonomy and
corresponding rubrics for better evaluating the generation of actions
([Wan et al., 2026](#bib.bib45)).

## 6 Conclusion

In this work, we introduce WebAggregator, a framework designed to bridge
the gap between information seeking and compositional reasoning in Deep
Research agents. Through the construction of WebAggregatorQA and the
WebAggregator models, we demonstrate that verifiable,
reasoning-intensive training data significantly boosts agent performance
across diverse benchmarks. Crucially, our analysis reveals a fundamental
bottleneck: accurate retrieval does not guarantee task success, as
current models struggle to integrate distributed information. By
mitigating these deficits through targeted fine-tuning, WebAggregator
paves the way for future research to transcend retrieval-centric
paradigms and move closer to autonomous scientific discovery.

## Limitations

To ensure a fair and controlled comparison, all evaluation protocols and
experimental details are strictly aligned with established methodologies
([Wu et al., 2025a](#bib.bib5); [Li et al., 2025b](#bib.bib9); [Wu et
al., 2025b](#bib.bib3); [Tao et al., 2025](#bib.bib10)), precluding any
interference from prior knowledge. Following these standards, we
evaluated WebAggregator across several well-recognized benchmarks
[Mialon et al. (2023)](#bib.bib2); [Wu et al. (2025b)](#bib.bib3); [Chen
et al. (2025)](#bib.bib14) to demonstrate its generalization
capabilities. Furthermore, we conducted a rigorous data contamination
analysis on WebAggregatorQA; as detailed in Appendix
[C](#A3 "Appendix C Data Contamination Analysis ‣ WebAggregator: Enhancing Compositional Reasoning Capabilities of Deep Research Agent Foundation Models"),
the results confirm zero overlap with existing benchmarks. Given our
automated pipeline, we implemented strict post-construction filtering
and utilized a rejection sampling procedure during training to eliminate
misaligned QA pairs, thereby guaranteeing high data quality. While the
data construction of WebAggregator requires environmental interaction
and execution time, it remains highly cost-effective compared to human
annotation, which often demands several hours of expert labor per task.
The code, data and models will be open-sourced.

|                                 |                                                                                         |
| ------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Operations                      | Questions                                                                               |
| Element Operations              | Aggregate elements/entities, e.g., numbers, times, names$`(x,y)`$.                      |
| Retrieve $`(x)`$                | In Amor: A Recipe for Building Adaptable … , what hourly pay (in USD) is                |
|                                 | for the hired NLP expert?                                                               |
| Inverse $`(x)`$                 | Which American actor won the Academy Award for XXX in the 1990s released                |
|                                 | their first solo studio album the greatest number of years after their Oscar win?       |
| Math $`(x,y)`$                  | Among Benedict, Robert Downey, and …, for the person’s first appearance in a            |
|                                 | Marvel Cinematic Universe film corresponded to the highest ROI for their                |

## Appendix A Agent Structure

|                     |                     |
| ------------------- | ------------------- |
| Action              | Observation         |
| Search(Query)       | Search results      |
| Visit(URL)          | Web Text & DOM      |
| StrFind(Query)      | Matched str in text |
| Input(str, tbox_id) | Web Text & DOM      |
| Click(button_id)    | Web Text & DOM      |
| Scroll(Pixels)      | Web Text & DOM      |
| Goback()            | Web Text & DOM      |
| FileRead(Path)      | File content        |
| Screenshot(Path)    | Capture screen      |
| ImageCaption(Path)  | Image description   |

Table 6: Action and Observation space.

First, we introduce our agent framework. User instructions often require
accessing diverse information on the web—plain text, images, or
files—some needing specific interactions like button clicks. Thus, the
agent must go beyond extracting static page text. We categorize tools by
information source: Search (Search), Static Page Parsing (Visit,
StrFind), Dynamic Interaction (Input, Click, Scroll, Goback), File
Processing (FileRead), and Image Captioning (ImageCaption).

Our implementation utilizes a code-based ReAct ([Yao et al.,
2023](#bib.bib13)) agent, built on SmolAgents ([Roucher et al.,
2025](#bib.bib12)), which outputs natural language thoughts,
Python-coded actions, and receives code log as environment observations.
Each task runs within a fixed 30-step budget, where a step includes an
agent action and its observation. We extend the opendeepresearch
SmolAgents instance with DOM parsing for finer web interactions (see
Table
[6](#A1.T6 "Table 6 ‣ Appendix A Agent Structure ‣ WebAggregator: Enhancing Compositional Reasoning Capabilities of Deep Research Agent Foundation Models")).
This web agent effectively handles tasks requiring information from
multiple sources, as summarized in Table
[2](#S1.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ WebAggregator: Enhancing Compositional Reasoning Capabilities of Deep Research Agent Foundation Models").

## Appendix B More Details for WebAggregatorQA

### B.1 More Explanations of Quality Control

##### QA Alignment-based Filtering

To improve data quality, we implemented a two-stage refinement process
for task construction. The first stage uses a self-refinement tool with
a checklist (Appendix
[B.5](#A2.SS5 "B.5 Prompt of Intergrated Data Quality Checking Tool ‣ Appendix B More Details for WebAggregatorQA ‣ WebAggregator: Enhancing Compositional Reasoning Capabilities of Deep Research Agent Foundation Models"))
to quickly verify and revise questions during creation. Items meeting
all criteria are accepted and outputted; those that don’t are revised
based on feedback until they comply. The second stage involves a data
checking agent that thoroughly reviews all reference URLs to ensure
alignment of question, answer, and sources (Appendix
[B.4](#A2.SS4 "B.4 Prompt of Data Quality Checking Agent ‣ Appendix B More Details for WebAggregatorQA ‣ WebAggregator: Enhancing Compositional Reasoning Capabilities of Deep Research Agent Foundation Models")).
About 11.72% of the data were filtered out for failing to meet these
standards.

![Refer to caption](2510.14438v2/web-explore.png)

Figure 10: A running example of Proactive Web Exploring: a greater
variety of interactions fosters a richer diversity of knowledge and
introduces more challenges throughout the process, e.g., questions built
from file knowledge also test the file-processing abilities of
responding agents.

##### Diversity Constraint

We ensure dataset diversity by balancing domain and aggregation
operation distributions. First, we annotated anchor URL domains with
GPT-4.1 and sampled data to achieve a more balanced domain distribution,
shown in Figure
[4](#S2.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 2.2.1 Proactive Explorer ‣ 2.2 WebAggregator: From Exploration to Composition ‣ 2 WebAggregator ‣ WebAggregator: Enhancing Compositional Reasoning Capabilities of Deep Research Agent Foundation Models").
Second, we analyzed compositional reasoning types using GPT-4.1 to
identify high- and low-level operations (e.g., math subtraction).
Although not perfectly reliable without solving the questions, common
operations like calculating average GDP can be accurately detected. We
then adjusted prompts to emphasize rare aggregation types, increasing
their sample frequency. Figure
[8](#A0.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ WebAggregator: Enhancing Compositional Reasoning Capabilities of Deep Research Agent Foundation Models")
shows a word cloud illustrating how different high-level aggregation
tasks yield diverse specific operations, such as intersection for set
operations and table processing for Science Analysis.

##### Data Leakage Avoidance

During proactive web exploration, agents may download and parse existing
datasets. To prevent data contamination, we created a website keyword
blacklist. Pages matching the blacklist or containing identified
datasets were excluded from retrieval and subsequent model evaluation to
ensure the fairness of the evaluation.

### B.2 Testset Annotation

#### B.2.1 Data Collection and Verification

The construction of the test set includes the seed tasks collection,
several rounds of revision, and cross-validation procedures. Three human
annotators are involved, all of them with at least a bachelor’s degree.
Each sample requires an average of 3 hours of annotation work, and the
whole procedure lasts for more than 4 weeks of part-time work (4 hours a
day).

Seed Tasks Collection A single human annotator, even if highly
specialized in one domain, faces inherent limitations in generating
diverse and comprehensive samples across multiple fields. To address
this, we engage multiple annotators to revise 200 topic-diverse tasks,
uniformly selected from WebAggregatorQA based on their domain labels.
These carefully revised seed examples help ensure that the test set
attains the desired diversity.

Task Revision Principles Our initial analysis, consistent with prior
work ([Wei et al., 2025](#bib.bib15)), shows that due to high
uncertainty in the web environment and an answer-to-question task
design, questions are generally well-structured but often lack unique
ground truths. While this ambiguity may be tolerable for training, it is
unacceptable for testing. Thus, our key revision principle is to ensure
each question is unambiguous and has exactly one correct answer.

- •
  QA (1) Ensure clarity in the question statements. All claims must be
  explicitly stated, and if multiple sources of evidence exist,
  additional constraints should be provided in the question to avoid
  ambiguity. (2) The reference answer must be the sole feasible and
  correct one to the question.
- •
  Reference Reference information, including URLs and solutions, is
  vital to the revision process. When these reference URLs and solutions
  are properly validated, the quality and reliability of the questions
  and answers are assured. Accordingly, annotators are required to: (1)
  verify the reliability of URLs, ensuring they originate from
  authoritative and reputable sources; (2) ensure consistency: the
  evidence remains stable and not prone to variation across different
  websites, contexts, or over time; (3) confirm the fidelity of URLs:
  each provided reference URL directly and substantively supports the
  question. Those pages that have a strict CAPTCHA will be replaced with
  more stable ones. Then the questions and answers are revised
  accordingly.

The second principle is to increase task complexity from the same two
perspectives: complex compositional reasoning and diversified
information sources. We provide annotators with the compositional
reasoning guidance and encourage them to incorporate more reasoning
steps into the questions to enhance their difficulty. They are also
advised to leverage various information forms beyond plain webpage text.
The answer should not be directly found on the web page.

![Refer to caption](2510.14438v2/mm-demo.png)

Figure 11: A multimodal sample from the test set of WebAggregatorQA. To
solve this task, the agent must extract information from the image to
obtain clues for the next step. Since the image is not provided with the
question, the agent is required to locate the relevant picture
independently.

Verification We utilize agents to assist the human validation procedure.
Initially, a GPT-4.1-powered agent attempts to solve the questions,
facilitating identification of potential ambiguities from the solver’s
perspective within a realistic web environment. Subsequently, human
annotators review the agent’s responses, detect any misunderstandings,
and revise the questions, solutions, and answers accordingly. This cycle
is repeated once more to ensure comprehensive disambiguation.

In the final stage, human annotators independently solve the tasks for
cross-validation purposes. Samples that fail to achieve consensus with
previously annotated answers are excluded. The independent annotation
achieved agreement with 155 out of 159 references, with 4 tasks omitted
due to excessive complexity, thereby validating the quality of the
references.

## Appendix C Data Contamination Analysis

We investigate potential data contamination between WebAggregatorQA and
GAIA through two similarity analyses, with the results presented in
Figure
[12](#A2.F12 "Figure 12 ‣ B.5 Prompt of Intergrated Data Quality Checking Tool ‣ Appendix B More Details for WebAggregatorQA ‣ WebAggregator: Enhancing Compositional Reasoning Capabilities of Deep Research Agent Foundation Models").
First, to establish a baseline, we prompt an LLM to paraphrase the GAIA
dataset, creating a new version termed GAIA-para. We then measure the
similarity between the original and paraphrased GAIA questions. Second,
we assess the cross-dataset overlap by sampling 100,000 pairs from the
Cartesian product of the WebAggregatorQA training set and GAIA and
computing their similarity. For all comparisons, we employ three
metrics: a semantic similarity score calculated by Qwen3-Embedding-8B,
ROUGE-L, and Jaccard similarity.

Figure
[12](#A2.F12 "Figure 12 ‣ B.5 Prompt of Intergrated Data Quality Checking Tool ‣ Appendix B More Details for WebAggregatorQA ‣ WebAggregator: Enhancing Compositional Reasoning Capabilities of Deep Research Agent Foundation Models")
reveals a stark contrast: while GAIA shows significant similarity with
its paraphrased counterpart, its overlap with WebAggregatorQA is
negligible. This provides strong evidence that our WebAggregatorQA
dataset is free from GAIA data contamination.
